A revision of Litvak’s conjecture on Gaussian minima and a volumetric zone conjecture

Dmitriy Kunisky Affiliation: Department of Applied Mathematics & Statistics, Johns Hopkins University
May 3, 2026
Abstract

Litvak (2018) conjectured that, for any p>0p>0, the quantity 𝔼⁡[mini=1n​|gi|p]\mathbb{E}[\min_{i=1}^{n}|g_{i}|^{p}] where g∼𝒩⁡(0,Σ)g\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma) is a centered Gaussian random vector is minimized among n×nn\times n correlation matrices Σ\Sigma by the Gram matrix of the regular simplex in ℝn−1\mathbb{R}^{n-1}. We disprove this conjecture: the matrix with entries Σi​jcos=cos⁡(π⁡(i−j)/n)\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}}_{ij}=\cos(\pi(i-j)/n) already achieves a smaller moment for p=2p=2 and n=4n=4. We propose that Σcos\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}} is in fact the correct minimizer of these moments for all p>0p>0 and n≥1n\geq 1. Towards proving this, we conjecture a volumetric extension of Fejes Tóth’s zone conjecture (1973), whose covering version was proved by Jiang and Polyanskii (2017). Conditional on this conjecture, we show the stronger result that mini=1n​|gi|\min_{i=1}^{n}|g_{i}| for g∼𝒩⁡(0,Σcos)g\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}}) is stochastically dominated by mini=1n​|hi|\min_{i=1}^{n}|h_{i}| for h∼𝒩⁡(0,Σ)h\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma) for any n×nn\times n correlation matrix Σ\Sigma. Our counterexample Σcos\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}} was found by the AlphaEvolve AI-assisted optimization system, and we also include a brief discussion of its application to such problems.

1 Introduction

Let z∼𝒩⁡(0,In)z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{n}) be a standard Gaussian vector. For an n×nn\times n correlation matrix Σ\Sigma (i.e., one having Σ⪰0\Sigma\succeq 0 and Σi​i=1\Sigma_{ii}=1 for each i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n), define the random variable

M(Σ):⁣=mini=1n|(Σ1/2z)i|.M(\Sigma)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\min_{i=1}^{n}|(\Sigma^{1/2}z)_{i}|.

Equivalently, if g∼𝒩⁡(0,Σ)g\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma), then M⁡(Σ)M(\Sigma) has the same law as mini=1n​|gi|\min_{i=1}^{n}|g_{i}|. The goal of this note is to consider, in various senses, what correlation matrix Σ\Sigma makes the random variable M⁡(Σ)M(\Sigma) as typically small as possible.

One natural choice, motivated by the solution (proven or conjectural) to many other such extremal questions (see below for citations), is the covariance given by the Gram matrix of a regular simplex in ℝn−1\mathbb{R}^{n-1},

ΣΔi​j:⁣={1if ​i=j,−1n−1if ​i≠j.\Sigma^{\Delta}_{ij}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\begin{cases}1&\text{if }i=j,\\ -\frac{1}{n-1}&\text{if }i\neq j.\end{cases}

The following conjecture claiming a specific sense in which this is true has, to the best of our knowledge, remained open since its proposal.

Conjecture 1.1 (Conjecture 5.1 of [Lit18]).

Let n≥3n\geq 3. For every n×nn\times n correlation matrix Σ\Sigma and p>0p>0,

𝔼⁡[M​(ΣΔ)p]≤𝔼⁡[M​(Σ)p].\mathbb{E}[M(\Sigma^{\Delta})^{p}]\leq\mathbb{E}[M(\Sigma)^{p}].

The conjecture is a natural companion to the better-known simplex mean width conjecture. That problem asks whether the regular simplex maximizes the mean width among simplices inscribed in the Euclidean ball. In Gaussian language, it asks whether the simplex covariance maximizes among correlation matrices the expectation of the largest coordinate of a Gaussian vector, 𝔼⁡[maxi=1n​gi]\mathbb{E}[\max_{i=1}^{n}g_{i}] in the above notation. The same note [Lit18] also discusses many similar problems, and formulates the similar Conjecture 1.1 motivated in part by considerations originating with a conjecture of Mallat–Zeitouni [MZ11].

The goal of the present note is to disprove this conjecture and propose a modification that we believe to be correct. Our counterexample to Conjecture 1.1 will use the covariance matrix

Σi​jcos:⁣=cos(π⁡(i−j)n) for 1≤i,j≤n,\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}}_{ij}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\cos\left(\frac{\pi(i-j)}{n}\right)\text{ for }1\leq i,j\leq n,

a rank-two correlation matrix, which already “beats” ΣΔ\Sigma^{\Delta} in the context of Conjecture 1.1 for n=4n=4 and p=2p=2. We visualize the matrices Σcos\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}} and ΣΔ\Sigma^{\Delta} in Figure 1.

Organization

The rest of the note is organized as follows. First, we prove that the above is indeed a counterexample to Conjecture 1.1 (Theorem 2.2). Second, we propose a strengthened version of Conjecture 1.1 with ΣΔ\Sigma^{\Delta} replaced by Σcos\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}} (Conjecture 3.1). Third, we propose an ancillary geometric conjecture (Conjecture 4.1) which implies our conjecture (Theorem 4.2). Finally, we give a brief discussion of the helpful and perhaps instructive role of artificial intelligence assistants and black-box optimization in our discovery of these results (Section 5.2).

Notation

We write 𝒩⁡(μ,Σ)\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma) for the multivariate Gaussian measure with mean μ\mu and covariance Σ\Sigma. We write 𝕊n−1​(r)⊂ℝn\mathbb{S}^{n-1}(r)\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} for the sphere of radius rr in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, and 𝕊n−1:⁣=𝕊n−1(1)\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\mathbb{S}^{n-1}(1) for the unit sphere.

2 Counterexample to Conjecture 1.1

We first discuss the structure of Σcos\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}} and M⁡(Σcos)M(\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}}). Define the vectors

vj:⁣=(cos((j−1)​πn),sin((j−1)​πn))∈ℝ2 for 1≤j≤n.v_{j}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\left(\cos\left(\frac{(j-1)\pi}{n}\right),\sin\left(\frac{(j-1)\pi}{n}\right)\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\text{ for }1\leq j\leq n.

These define lines whose intersection points with the unit circle in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} are the vertices of a regular 2​n2n-gon. Σcos\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}} is the Gram matrix of these vectors vjv_{j}, Σi​jcos=⟨vi,vj⟩\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}}_{ij}=\langle v_{i},v_{j}\rangle. Thus, if z∼𝒩⁡(0,I2)z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{2}) and we define

hk:⁣=⟨z,vk⟩,h_{k}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\langle z,v_{k}\rangle,

then hh has the law 𝒩⁡(0,Σcos)\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}}). The law of the associated minimum random variable therefore can be realized as

M⁡(Σcos)=(d)min1≤j≤n⁡|⟨z,vj⟩|.M(\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{(d)}}}{{=}}\min_{1\leq j\leq n}|\langle z,v_{j}\rangle|.
Proposition 2.1 (Law of M⁡(Σcos)M(\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}})).

Let r2∼χ2​(2)r^{2}\sim\chi^{2}(2) and θ∼Unif⁡([0,π2​n])\theta\sim\Unif([0,\frac{\pi}{2n}]) be independent.11 1 The law of such rr is also sometimes called the Rayleigh distribution. Then, M⁡(Σcos)M(\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}}) has the same law as r​sin⁡(θ)r\sin(\theta). Consequently, for all t,p>0t,p>0 we have

ℙ[M(Σcos)≥t]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[M(\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}})\geq t] =2​nπ​∫0π2​nexp⁡(−t22​sin2⁡θ)​𝑑θ,\displaystyle=\frac{2n}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2n}}\exp\left(-\frac{t^{2}}{2\sin^{2}\theta}\right)\,d\theta,
𝔼⁡[M​(Σcos)p]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[M(\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}})^{p}] =2p/2​Γ​(1+p2)​2​nπ​∫0π2​nsinp⁡θ​𝑑θ.\displaystyle=2^{p/2}\Gamma\left(1+\frac{p}{2}\right)\frac{2n}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2n}}\sin^{p}\theta\,d\theta.
Proof.

Let z∼𝒩⁡(0,I2)z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{2}). Write this vector as z=(r​cos⁡ϕ,r​sin⁡ϕ)z=(r\cos\phi,r\sin\phi) in polar coordinates. We have r2=z12+z22r^{2}=z_{1}^{2}+z_{2}^{2} has law χ2​(2)\chi^{2}(2), ϕ\phi is uniformly distributed with law Unif⁡([0,2​π])\Unif([0,2\pi]), and the two are independent by a standard property of Gaussian random vectors. Since absolute values identify angles modulo π\pi, the nn lines perpendicular to the vkv_{k} divide the upper semicircle of the unit circle in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} into nn equal arcs. The angular distance θ\theta from ϕ\phi to nearest such perpendicular line therefore has law Unif⁡([0,π2​n])\Unif([0,\frac{\pi}{2n}]). By construction, we then have

M⁡(Σcos)=(d)mink⁡|⟨z,vk⟩|=r​sin⁡(θ).M(\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{(d)}}}{{=}}\min_{k}|\langle z,v_{k}\rangle|=r\sin(\theta).

The tail and moment formulas follow from the independence of rr and θ\theta and explicit formulas for their densities. ∎

Theorem 2.2 (Counterexample to Conjecture 1.1).

For n=4n=4, we have

𝔼⁡[M​(Σcos)2]<𝔼⁡[M​(ΣΔ)2].\mathbb{E}[M(\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}})^{2}]<\mathbb{E}[M(\Sigma^{\Delta})^{2}].

Thus Conjecture 1.1 is false for n=4n=4 and p=2p=2.

Proof.

This is simple to verify by a numerical computation, but let us give a careful rigorous justification for the sake of completeness. By Proposition 2.1, we may compute exactly

𝔼⁡[M​(Σcos)2]=1−n​sin⁡(π/n)π.\mathbb{E}[M(\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}})^{2}]=1-\frac{n\sin(\pi/n)}{\pi}.

For n=4n=4, this is

1−2​2π∈[0.099683,0.099684].1-\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\pi}\in[0.099683,0.099684].

It remains to bound the same expectation for the simplex covariance from below. For n=4n=4, realize the simplex covariance as the Gram matrix Σi​jΔ=⟨ui,uj⟩\Sigma^{\Delta}_{ij}=\langle u_{i},u_{j}\rangle for

u1=(1,1,1)3,u2=(1,−1,−1)3,u3=(−1,1,−1)3,u4=(−1,−1,1)3.u_{1}=\frac{(1,1,1)}{\sqrt{3}},\quad u_{2}=\frac{(1,-1,-1)}{\sqrt{3}},\quad u_{3}=\frac{(-1,1,-1)}{\sqrt{3}},\quad u_{4}=\frac{(-1,-1,1)}{\sqrt{3}}.

Let g∼𝒩⁡(0,I3)g\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{3}) and write g=(r​w1,r​w2,r​w3)g=(rw_{1},rw_{2},rw_{3}) in spherical coordinates in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}. Then rr and ww are independent, 𝔼⁡[r2]=3\mathbb{E}[r^{2}]=3, and

M⁡(ΣΔ)=r​mini​|⟨w,ui⟩|.M(\Sigma^{\Delta})=r\min_{i}|\langle w,u_{i}\rangle|.

By the sign-change and coordinate-permutation symmetries of the set of lines spanned by the uiu_{i}, it suffices to integrate over the sector w1≥w2≥w3≥0w_{1}\geq w_{2}\geq w_{3}\geq 0 of the sphere 𝕊2={w∈ℝ3:w12+w22+w32=1}\mathbb{S}^{2}=\{w\in\mathbb{R}^{3}:w_{1}^{2}+w_{2}^{2}+w_{3}^{2}=1\}. On this sector,

mini⁡|⟨(w1,w2,w3),ui⟩|=|w1−w2−w3|3.\min_{i}|\langle(w_{1},w_{2},w_{3}),u_{i}\rangle|=\frac{|w_{1}-w_{2}-w_{3}|}{\sqrt{3}}.

Using the chart for this sector

(w1,w2,w3)=(1,s,s​t)1+s2+s2​t2,s,t∈[0,1](w_{1},w_{2},w_{3})=\frac{(1,s,st)}{\sqrt{1+s^{2}+s^{2}t^{2}}},\qquad s,t\in[0,1]

and multiplying the integral over the sector by the 23⋅3!=482^{3}\cdot 3!=48 congruent sectors, we get the concrete integral expression

𝔼⁡[M​(ΣΔ)2]=12π​∫01∫01s​(1−s−s​t)2(1+s2+s2​t2)5/2​𝑑s​𝑑t.\mathbb{E}[M(\Sigma^{\Delta})^{2}]=\frac{12}{\pi}\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{s(1-s-st)^{2}}{(1+s^{2}+s^{2}t^{2})^{5/2}}\,ds\,dt.

Subdividing the unit square into 400×400400\times 400 boxes and computing interval arithmetic bounds on this integral numerically gives

𝔼⁡[M​(ΣΔ)2]∈[0.139622,0.144779].\mathbb{E}[M(\Sigma^{\Delta})^{2}]\in[0.139622,0.144779].

This lower bound is larger than 1−2​2/π1-2\sqrt{2}/\pi, completing the proof. ∎

3 Strengthened revision of Conjecture 1.1

We further believe that the cosine covariance is the true optimizer in Conjecture 1.1, and that this holds in a stronger sense than moment comparison. We propose the following revision of the Conjecture:

Conjecture 3.1.

For every n≥1n\geq 1, every correlation matrix Σ\Sigma, and every t≥0t\geq 0,

ℙ[M(Σcos)≥t]≤ℙ[M(Σ)≥t].\mathbb{P}[M(\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}})\geq t]\leq\mathbb{P}[M(\Sigma)\geq t].

That is, M⁡(Σcos)M(\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}}) is stochastically dominated by M⁡(Σ)M(\Sigma). In particular,

𝔼⁡[M​(Σcos)p]≤𝔼⁡[M​(Σ)p]\mathbb{E}[M(\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}})^{p}]\leq\mathbb{E}[M(\Sigma)^{p}]

for every p>0p>0.

This phenomenon is illustrated in Figure 2, which plots the tail probabilities in question for covariances Σcos\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}}, ΣΔ\Sigma^{\Delta}, the identity matrix, and many independent draws of random full- and low-rank correlation matrices (formed as Gram matrices of independent unit vectors of suitable dimension). We note that the tail probability function of Σcos\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}} seems to be an “outlier” in the space of correlation matrices, with exceptional decay much faster than either of the other fixed examples and than typical random covariances.

4 Volumetric zone conjecture

We have not been able to prove Conjecture 3.1. However, we can reduce it to the following geometric conjecture in the spirit of the Fejes Tóth zone conjecture [Tót73]—now the Jiang–Polyanskii theorem [JP17]—and other similar results. See Section 5.1 for more references.

Conjecture 4.1 (Volumetric zone conjecture).

Let d≥2d\geq 2, let u1,…,un∈𝕊d−1u_{1},\dots,u_{n}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}, and let α∈[0,π/2]\alpha\in[0,\pi/2]. For a unit vector uu, define the spherical zone

Z(u,α):⁣={v∈𝕊d−1:|⟨v,u⟩|≤sin(α)}.Z(u,\alpha)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\{v\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}:|\langle v,u\rangle|\leq\sin(\alpha)\}.

For j=1,…,nj=1,\dots,n, define

vj:⁣=(cos((j−1)​πn),sin((j−1)​πn),0,…,0)∈𝕊d−1.v_{j}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\left(\cos\left(\frac{(j-1)\pi}{n}\right),\sin\left(\frac{(j-1)\pi}{n}\right),0,\dots,0\right)\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}.

Then

σd−1​(⋃j=1nZ⁡(uj,α))≤σd−1​(⋃j=1nZ⁡(vj,α)),\sigma_{d-1}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^{n}Z(u_{j},\alpha)\right)\leq\sigma_{d-1}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^{n}Z(v_{j},\alpha)\right),

where σd−1\sigma_{d-1} denotes the surface measure on 𝕊d−1\mathbb{S}^{d-1} normalized to be a probability measure.

The conjecture says that among nn equal-width zones on the sphere, the zones around nn evenly-spaced great subspheres sharing a subsphere of codimension two maximize the surface measure of the union. The original zone conjecture of [Tót73], proved by [JP17], asked for the minimum width 2​α2\alpha required for the union of nn spherical zones to cover the entire sphere, claiming that the minimum is achieved by the same configuration. Our conjecture may be viewed as generalizing this to “thinner” configurations of zones that only cover a given fraction of the sphere. We visualize the conjectural optimal configuration in Figure 3.

This conjecture implies our conjecture on Gaussian minima:

Theorem 4.2.

Conjecture 4.1 implies Conjecture 3.1.

Proof.

The cases n=1n=1 and t=0t=0 of Conjecture 3.1 are trivial, so suppose n≥2n\geq 2 and t>0t>0. Suppose Conjecture 4.1 holds. Choose unit vectors u1,…,unu_{1},\dots,u_{n} in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} whose Gram matrix is Σ\Sigma, i.e., having Σi​j=⟨ui,uj⟩\Sigma_{ij}=\langle u_{i},u_{j}\rangle. Let g∼𝒩⁡(0,In)g\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{n}). Then

(⟨g,u1⟩,…,⟨g,un⟩)∼𝒩⁡(0,Σ),(\langle g,u_{1}\rangle,\dots,\langle g,u_{n}\rangle)\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma),

so

M⁡(Σ)=(d)minj=1n​|⟨g,uj⟩|.M(\Sigma)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{(d)}}}{{=}}\min_{j=1}^{n}|\langle g,u_{j}\rangle|.

For t>0t>0, define the union of slabs

B(t):⁣=⋃j=1n{v∈ℝn:|⟨v,uj⟩|≤t}.B(t)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\bigcup_{j=1}^{n}\{v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:|\langle v,u_{j}\rangle|\leq t\}.

Then

ℙ[M(Σ)≤t]=γn(B(t)),\mathbb{P}[M(\Sigma)\leq t]=\gamma_{n}(B(t)),

where γn=𝒩⁡(0,In)\gamma_{n}=\mathcal{N}(0,I_{n}) is the standard Gaussian measure on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}.

Write S(t,r):⁣=B(t)∩𝕊n−1(r)S(t,r)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}B(t)\cap\mathbb{S}^{n-1}(r), the intersection of this union of slabs with the sphere of radius rr. When t/r≥1t/r\geq 1, S⁡(t,r)=𝕊n−1​(r)S(t,r)=\mathbb{S}^{n-1}(r). When 0<t/r<10<t/r<1, we have by definition

S⁡(t,r)=r⋅⋃j=1nZ⁡(uj,arcsin⁡(tr)).S(t,r)=r\cdot\bigcup_{j=1}^{n}Z\left(u_{j},\arcsin\left(\frac{t}{r}\right)\right).

Thus, defining

α(t,r):⁣={π/2if ​r≤t,arcsin⁡(t/r)if ​r>t\alpha(t,r)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\begin{cases}\pi/2&\text{if }r\leq t,\\ \arcsin(t/r)&\text{if }r>t\end{cases}

we compute

ℙ[M(Σ)≤t]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[M(\Sigma)\leq t] =γn​(B​(t))\displaystyle=\gamma_{n}(B(t))
=ℙg∼𝒩⁡(0,In)[g∈B(t)]\displaystyle=\mathop{\mathbb{P}}_{g\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{n})}[g\in B(t)]
=ℙg∼𝒩⁡(0,In)[g∈S(t,∥g∥)]\displaystyle=\mathop{\mathbb{P}}_{g\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{n})}[g\in S(t,\|g\|)]
=ℙg∼𝒩⁡(0,In)[g‖g‖∈⋃j=1nZ(uj,α(t,∥g∥))]\displaystyle=\mathop{\mathbb{P}}_{g\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{n})}\left[\frac{g}{\|g\|}\in\bigcup_{j=1}^{n}Z\left(u_{j},\alpha(t,\|g\|)\right)\right]
and since ‖g‖\|g\| is independent of g/‖g‖g/\|g\| and the latter has law σn−1\sigma_{n-1}, we have
=𝔼g∼𝒩⁡(0,In)[σn−1​(⋃j=1nZ⁡(uj,α⁡(t,‖g‖)))]\displaystyle=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{g\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{n})}\left[\sigma_{n-1}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^{n}Z\left(u_{j},\alpha(t,\|g\|)\right)\right)\right]
and letting viv_{i} be as in Conjecture 4.1 and using that we assume the conjecture holds,
≤𝔼g∼𝒩⁡(0,In)[σn−1​(⋃j=1nZ⁡(vj,α⁡(t,‖g‖)))]\displaystyle\leq\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{g\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{n})}\left[\sigma_{n-1}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^{n}Z\left(v_{j},\alpha(t,\|g\|)\right)\right)\right]
and reversing the same manipulations
=ℙ[M(Σcos)≤t],\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}[M(\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}})\leq t],

giving the result since the law of M⁡(Σ)M(\Sigma) does not have atoms for any correlation matrix Σ\Sigma. The result on moments follows by the standard manipulation of expressing the expectations as integrals over the tail probabilities. ∎

5 Discussion

5.1 Related work

Conjecture 1.1 appears as Conjecture 5.1 in Litvak’s survey [Lit18] on the simplex mean width conjecture (which is Conjecture 1.4 of the survey). Litvak presents it as part of a family of Gaussian extremal problems related to simplex covariances, including the mean-width problem, the simplex code conjecture, and various related geometric claims.

One motivation for Conjecture 1.1 comes from a conjecture of Mallat and Zeitouni on the Karhunen–Loève basis in nonlinear reconstruction [MZ11]. Litvak notes that the original intuition behind that problem would have followed from a stronger statement about minima with p=2p=2 for which the identity covariance was proposed as optimal. The same discussion records that van Handel gave an example showing that, in the three-variable case, the simplex covariance improves on the identity covariance. While the original conjecture of Mallat–Zeitouni remains open, it was later resolved by Litvak and Tikhomirov up to absolute constants [LT18].

The estimates of Gordon, Litvak, Schütt, and Werner on minima of Gaussian and more general random variables give another nearby point of comparison [GLSW05, GLSW06]. Those works give sharp-order bounds for minima and order statistics under broad assumptions. The present problem is different in that the marginal variances are fixed and the covariance matrix itself is the object to optimize.

The geometric input proposed here is a volumetric variant of Fejes Tóth’s zone problem [Tót73]. Jiang and Polyanskii proved the covering version of Fejes Tóth’s conjecture in all dimensions [JP17]. Ortega-Moreno gave a different proof for the equal-width case [OM21], and Zhao later streamlined that argument [Zha22]. Glazyrin, Karasev, and Polyanskii developed polynomial plank methods which also give a strengthening for spherical segments [GKP23]. For a broader view of plank problems and their applications, see Verreault’s survey [Ver22]. While Conjecture 4.1 seems like a natural generalization, to the best of our knowledge it has not appeared in the literature.

5.2 AI assistance

Our Σcos\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}} counterexample was found by black-box minimization of the functions fp​(Σ)=𝔼⁡[M​(Σ)p]f_{p}(\Sigma)=\mathbb{E}[M(\Sigma)^{p}] using AlphaEvolve [NVE+25], an optimization system based on code generation with large language models (see, e.g., [NRT25, NRT26] for other recent results obtained using it). After AlphaEvolve surfaced Σcos\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}} it was easy to recognize (for instance from a plot like in Figure 1) that there was an underlying continuous function, and then to identify it as the cosine. Experimenting with minimizing gt(Σ)=ℙ[M(Σ)≥t]g_{t}(\Sigma)=\mathbb{P}[M(\Sigma)\geq t] led to the stronger formulation of Conjecture 3.1.

Afterwards, we also considered whether more conventional optimization methods such as differential evolution and BFGS-type gradient methods could find the same optimizer. While these often gave improvements on the simplex covariance that would just as well disprove Conjecture 1.1, they only rarely converged to (what we believe is) the true minimizer Σcos\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}}, especially for nn larger than the dimension of the smallest counterexample n=4n=4 (for n=3n=3, M⁡(Σcos)M(\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}}) and M⁡(ΣΔ)M(\Sigma^{\Delta}) have the same law up to a coordinate sign change) and especially when optimizing the gtg_{t} functions which we evaluate by estimating the probabilities empirically.22 2 When run over only rank-two correlation matrices, these simpler methods did often find Σcos\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}}; however, this is a rather unrealistic point of comparison since we did not know before seeing the result of AlphaEvolve that the optimizer should be of such low rank. We also found that both the fpf_{p} and gtg_{t} functions can have spurious local minimizers different than the global minimizer Σcos\Sigma^{\mathrm{cos}}. Thus, aside from convenience of implementation, AlphaEvolve seems to offer an advantage as a research tool in this setting. In general, inspecting the output of AlphaEvolve or similar systems by hand to look for tractable structure seems to be a useful further step to translate its results into mathematical insights. It is an intriguing question whether this process itself could be automated to further accelerate research assisted with black-box optimization.

We also remark that the connection with the Fejes Tóth zone conjecture and related literature was unknown to us until it was surfaced by GPT-5.5 Pro when asked to prove Conjecture 3.1. On the other hand, this model repeatedly produced proofs which used that Conjecture as if it were included in the results of Fejes Tóth or others cited above. Its mistake was nonetheless informative: once the unsupported step was isolated, it pointed directly to the reasonable and independently interesting Conjecture 4.1.
